title: Turkey, Trots, and Touchdowns: How Thanksgiving Traditions Began
summary:
Turkey and touchdowns: Thanksgiving is packed with traditions.

Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November. It traces its roots to a harvest feast shared by European settlers and Native Americans in 1621. This year, it falls on November 26.

The first feast likely featured geese and ducks, but turkey has become the centerpiece of the meal. Writer Sarah Josepha Hale promoted turkey as the main dish, and turkeys were easy to raise and large enough to feed a crowd.

Cranberry sauce was already popular in New England, but cookbook author Amelia Simmons first suggested serving it with roast turkey in 1796. Nearly 70 years later, General Ulysses S. Grant reportedly ordered it for soldiers at Thanksgiving in 1864. Soon, turkey with cranberry sauce was a tradition nationwide.

Thanksgiving morning means turkey trots: races where runners dress in costumes and raise money for local charities. It began in 1896, when six friends organized a race in Buffalo, New York. Now in its 131st year, the Buffalo Turkey Trot is the world's oldest continuously run footrace, an 8K race that attracts 14,000 runners a year.

Then there is the Presidential Turkey Pardon at the White House, where the president officially spares a turkey from the holiday dinner. Its origin is unclear, though some trace it to Abraham Lincoln. It took its current form in 1989, when President George H.W. Bush formally pardoned a turkey.

Football rounds out the day. The NFL's Thanksgiving tradition began in 1934, when the Detroit Lions played the Chicago Bears to draw fans. The Lions have hosted a game every Thanksgiving since, except for a six-year break during World War II. The Dallas Cowboys joined in 1966, and the NFL later added a third game. In 2025, the three games averaged 44.7 million viewers, a record.
why_it_matters: Thanksgiving traditions shape how millions of American families spend one of the year's biggest holidays, and knowing where they came from shows how small choices — a writer's praise, a team's game, a few friends' race — can grow into customs shared across a whole country.

background_read: Thanksgiving is a holiday in the United States when families gather for a big meal and give thanks for what they have.
It grew out of a harvest feast shared by European settlers and Native Americans, and over time it picked up foods, races, and games that families now repeat every year.

Many of its traditions started small — a writer praising turkey, a few friends organizing a race, a football team playing to draw fans — and then spread across the country until they became part of the holiday itself.
That is why the day now mixes food, sport, and ceremony: each tradition was added by different people at different times, and each one stuck.
